newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-COVENTRY PLAN YET ANOTHER GREAT ESCAPE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-COVENTRY PLAN YET ANOTHER GREAT ESCAPE.

text.p: Liverpool's surprise 2-1 home defeat by Coventry on Sunday may have handed the English title initiative to Manchester United but for the victors the three points gained had a major impact on the opposite end of the table.
The win lifted Coventry from last place to 17th -- one above the drop zone -- and they could well defy the odds yet again and stay up.
It is no surprise to find Coventry deeply embroiled in the battle to avoid relegation -- the Midlands club's annual escape act has become almost a routine part of the end-of-season excitement.
But while everyone is aware of their constant fight to preserve their top-flight status, it is often overlooked that they belong to an elite group of clubs.

The Highfield Road outfit, formed in 1883, hope to complete a 30-year stay in the top division, which started when they gained promotion in 1967 and is bettered only by Arsenal, Everton and Liverpool.

Their manager on that occasion was current television analyst Jimmy Hill who, in his six-year spell, led the club to one of their most successful periods after they had won the second division championship in 1964.

This season, following last year's narrow escape when they avoided relegation only on goal difference, the club were expected to feature in the top half of the division under the leadership of experienced manager Ron Atkinson and new assistant Gordon Strachan.

With players of the calibre of former England international John Salako, ex-Manchester United striker Dion Dublin and veteran goalkeeper Steve Ogrizovic, blended with new three-million-pound ($4.9-million) signing Scotland captain Gary McAllister from Leeds, the promise seemed realistic.
But that has not been the case as the disappointing results at the start of the season saw a management reshuffle. "We certainly expected to do a lot better," says Ogrizovic.
In November, former Scotland international Strachan became manager as Atkinson moved into the role of director of football but this was not enough to turn around fortunes at the club.
At least not until they signed striker Darren Huckerby for one million pounds and defender Gary Breen for a club record 2.3 million pounds.
In fact, Huckerby looked as though he could save the club as he banged in the goals and led Coventry as high as 12th in early January.
But between then and Sunday's stunning Anfield success they managed just one league win and went into freefall -- collecting stinging condemnation for lack of heart along the way.

"There is more tension when you are at the bottom because it's all doom and gloom if teams get relegated," said Ogrizovic, who was in goal when Coventry won the F.A. Cup in 1987 -- their only major honour.

"It's worse at the bottom but the tension is there in all football matches. You can't allow yourself to worry too much. You have to concentrate on the games and it's as simple as that," added the goalkeeper.
No-one really knows what the problem is but Ogrizovic is convinced is does not lie in the weakness of Coventry's defence or at the feet of Strachan.
"I think to be quite honest we have got some talented defenders and if we look at it in comparison with other clubs around us it's favourable," he said.
"Gordon demands hard work from the players. He won't ask people to do more than they can but if you give him everything he is happy with that."
It would be a sad chapter in the history of Coventry if they were relegated but Sunday's success has rejuvenated everyone at the club.

"Each season usually throws up a daft weekend and this is it," said Strachan, who is already well versed in the language of relegation. "The better team didn't win today but what we've done is give ourselves a realistic chance of avoiding relegation." ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
